claim: Approximately 35% of women with Gestational Diabetes (GDM) progress to Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) within 10 years.
source: Approximately, 35% of women with Gestational Diabetes (GDM) progress to Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) within 10 years.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this statistic.

claim: 311 lipids were positively associated with T2D risk in women with recent GDM at 6-9 weeks postpartum.
source: We discovered 311 lipids positively and 70 lipids negatively associated with T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 70 lipids were negatively associated with T2D risk in women with recent GDM at 6-9 weeks postpartum.
source: We discovered 311 lipids positively and 70 lipids negatively associated with T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upregulation of glycerolipid metabolism involving triacylglycerol and diacylglycerol biosynthesis suggests activated lipid storage before diabetes onset.
source: The upregulation of glycerolipid metabolism involving triacylglycerol and diacylglycerol biosynthesis suggested activated lipid storage before diabetes onset.
evidence: This claim is based on pathway analysis of the lipidomics data and represents an interpretation of the biological significance.

claim: Decreased sphingomyelins, hexosylceramide and lactosylceramide indicate impaired sphingolipid metabolism in women who progress from GDM to T2D.
source: In contrast, decreased sphingomyelines, hexosylceramide and lactosylceramide indicated impaired sphingolipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is based on lipidomics data showing decreased levels of these lipid species and interpretation of their biological significance.

claim: A lipid signature was identified to effectively predict future diabetes risk in women with recent GDM.
source: Additionally, a lipid signature was identified to effectively predict future diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by predictive modeling using selected lipids from the dataset.

claim: Endogenous lipogenesis may be a driving force for future diabetes onset in women with GDM.
source: These findings demonstrate an underlying dyslipidemia during the early postpartum in those GDM women who progress to T2D and suggest endogenous lipogenesis may be a driving force for future diabetes onset.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on interpretation of the lipid profile changes observed in the study.

claim: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) affects 1–14% of all pregnancies depending on diagnostic criteria and population characteristics.
source: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) develops during pregnancy, affecting 1–14% of all pregnancies depending on diagnostic criteria and the population characteristics (Chen et al., 2018; Melchior et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Women with a history of GDM are approximately 7 times more likely to develop type 2 diabetes (T2D) during the child-bearing years compared to women who had no previous GDM.
source: However, women with a history of GDM are ~7 times more likely to develop type 2 diabetes (T2D) during the child-bearing years compared to women who had no previous GDM (Chen et al., 2018; Bellamy et al., 2009; Gunderson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 35–50% of women with GDM may progress to T2D within 10 years after delivery.
source: In fact, it is estimated that 35–50% of women with GDM may progress to T2D within 10 years after delivery (Bellamy et al., 2009; Tobias, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Within 15 to 25 years, the lifetime maternal risk for overt diabetes is estimated to reach >50% in women with GDM.
source: Within 15 to 25 years, the lifetime maternal risk for overt diabetes is estimated to reach >50% (American Diabetes Association, 2019; Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The SWIFT cohort enrolled a total of 1035 women diagnosed with GDM.
source: The SWIFT cohort enrolled a total of 1035 women diagnosed with GDM.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 1010 women in the SWIFT cohort did not have T2D at 6–9 weeks postpartum (baseline).
source: Of these, 1010 did not have T2D at 6–9 weeks postpartum (baseline) and 989 had follow up testing for glucose tolerance up to 8 years post-baseline.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 197 women in the SWIFT cohort developed incident T2D during the follow-up period.
source: During the follow-up period, 197 women had developed incident T2D and 791 did not (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 171 women with incident T2D cases had available plasma samples at baseline for lipidomics profiling.
source: In our current study, 171 women with incident T2D cases had available plasma samples at baseline, and 179 controls who did not develop T2D in 8 years' follow-up (350 participants in total) were profiled for lipidomics.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: A total of 1008 lipid species from 15 lipid classes as well as 296 fatty acids were assessed in the plasma samples.
source: A total of 1008 lipid species from 15 lipid classes as well as 296 fatty acids were assessed in the plasma samples of all participants (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Women who developed T2D had a higher percentage of insulin or oral medication treatment during pregnancy compared to controls (p<0.001).
source: Compared to the control group, a higher percentage of participants who developed T2D later on had been treated with insulin or oral medications during pregnancy (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: Prenatal 3 hr 100 g OGTT glucose z-scores were higher in the incident T2D case group than the control group (p<0.001).
source: Prenatal 3 hr 100 g OGTT (sum of the 4 z-scores for glucose values; fasting, 1 hr, 2 hr and 3 hr post-load, p<0.001) for the incident T2D case group were higher than the control group.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: At 6–9 weeks postpartum, women in the incident T2D group had higher mean FPG compared to controls (p<0.001).
source: At 6–9 weeks postpartum, compared to controls, women in the incident T2D group had higher mean FPG (p<0.001), 2hPG (p<0.001), fasting insulin (p=0.001), 2 hr insulin (p<0.001), fasting TAG (p=0.003), median HOMA-IR (p<0.001) and hypertension (p=0.04), but lower mean fasting HDL-C (p=0.017).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: At 6–9 weeks postpartum, women in the incident T2D group had higher mean 2hPG compared to controls (p<0.001).
source: At 6–9 weeks postpartum, compared to controls, women in the incident T2D group had higher mean FPG (p<0.001), 2hPG (p<0.001), fasting insulin (p=0.001), 2 hr insulin (p<0.001), fasting TAG (p=0.003), median HOMA-IR (p<0.001) and hypertension (p=0.04), but lower mean fasting HDL-C (p=0.017).

evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

source: At 6–9 weeks postpartum, compared to controls, women in the incident T2D group had higher mean FPG (p<0.001), 2hPG (p<0.001), fasting insulin (p=0.001), 2 hr insulin (p<0.001), fasting TAG (p=0.003), median HOMA-IR (p<0.001) and hypertension (p=0.04), but lower mean fasting HDL-C (p=0.017).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: Of the 816 lipid species analyzed, 311 were positively and 70 were negatively associated with T2D risk (FDR < 0.05).
source: Of the 816 lipid species, 311 were positively and 70 were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of lipidomics data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Of the 311 lipids positively associated with T2D risk, 293 were from TAG class, 17 from DAG class, and one from PE class.
source: Of the 311 lipids positively associated with risk, 293 were from TAG class while 17 from DAG class and one from PE class (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Of the 70 lipids negatively associated with T2D, 31 were from SM class, 27 from PC class, seven from CE class, four from FFA class and one from TAG class.
source: Of the 70 lipids negatively associated with T2D, 31 were from SM class, 27 from PC class, seven from CE class, four from FFA class and one from TAG class (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: 57.2% of all TAG species measured (293 out of 512 TAG) were significantly positively associated with T2D risk.
source: Most notably, 57.2% of all TAG species measured (293 out of 512 TAG) were significantly positively associated with T2D risk (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 17 out of 54 DAGs were upregulated in association with T2D risk.
source: Additionally, 17 out of 54 DAGs, intermediates of TAG synthesis, were upregulated, further suggesting TAG biosynthesis was abnormally active (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 40% (22 out of 55) measured PC were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: In contrast, 40% (22 out of 55) measured PC and 25% (3 out of 12) measured LPC were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 25% (3 out of 12) measured LPC were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: In contrast, 40% (22 out of 55) measured PC and 25% (3 out of 12) measured LPC were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 62% measured sphingolipids (31 out of 50) were inversely associated with T2D risk.
source: Similarly, 62% measured sphingolipids (31 out of 50) were inversely associated with T2D risk, particularly in classes of HCER (6 out of 9), LCER (9 out of 10) and sphingomyelins (10 out of 12) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 107 lipids were significantly associated with T2D progression at FDR < 0.001.
source: More strictly, by using a cut-off of FDR < 0.001, we demonstrated 107 lipids were significantly associated with T2D progression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of lipidomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 97 TAGs spanning carbon atom numbers from 42 to 56 with double bonds from 0 to 8 were consistently associated with increased diabetes risk.
source: In this panel, 97 TAGs spanning carbon atom numbers from 42 to 56 with double bonds from 0 to 8, along with one saturated DAG(16:0/16:0) were consistently associated with increased diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One saturated DAG(16:0/16:0) was consistently associated with increased diabetes risk.
source: In this panel, 97 TAGs spanning carbon atom numbers from 42 to 56 with double bonds from 0 to 8, along with one saturated DAG(16:0/16:0) were consistently associated with increased diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One monounsaturated PC(17:0/18:1) and three polyunsaturated PC species were inversely associated with future diabetes risk.
source: One monounsaturated PC(17:0/18:1) and three polyunsaturated PC(17:0/18:2), PC(18:1/20:4), PC(18:2/16:1) were inversely associated with future diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SM (18:1), SM(20:1), SM(24:1), HCER(24:1), and LCER(16:0) from the sphingolipid class were negatively associated with diabetes risk.
source: Similarly, SM (18:1), SM(20:1), SM(24:1), HCER(24:1), and LCER(16:0) from the sphingolipid class were negatively associated with diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TAGs and DAG demonstrated a weak to moderate positive correlation with fasting insulin and HOMA-IR.
source: TAGs and DAG demonstrated a weak to moderate positive correlation with fasting insulin and HOMA-IR while sphingolipids and phospholipids were shown to have a weak negative correlation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sphingolipids and phospholipids showed a weak negative correlation with fasting insulin and HOMA-IR.
source: TAGs and DAG demonstrated a weak to moderate positive correlation with fasting insulin and HOMA-IR while sphingolipids and phospholipids were shown to have a weak negative correlation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 107 T2D-associated lipids showed little correlation with 2hPG, age and BMI.
source: In contrast, those 107 lipids showed little correlation with 2hPG, age and BMI (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TAGs significantly associated with diabetes risk contained between 40–56 carbon atoms and 0–8 double bonds.
source: Among all the TAGs detected (carbon atoms from 36 to 60), those significantly associated with diabetes risk contained between 40–56 carbon atoms and 0–8 double bonds.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TAGs most significantly associated with T2D risk were clustered in the range of carbon atoms 50–54 and double bond 0–4, particularly with even carbon atoms 52 and 54.
source: TAGs most significantly associated with T2D risk were clustered in the range of carbon atoms 50–54 and double bond 0–4, particularly with even carbon atoms 52 and 54 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DAGs with an even number of carbon atoms 30, 32, 34, 36 but not odd numbers were associated with diabetes risk more prominently.
source: DAGs with an even number of carbon atoms 30, 32, 34, 36 but not odd numbers were associated with diabetes risk more prominently.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Three SFAs (FA12:0, FA14:0 and FA16:0) were positively associated with T2D risk.
source: For total fatty acids, three SFAs (FA12:0, FA14:0 and FA16:0) as well as a PUFA (FA18:3) were positively associated with T2D risk and two very long chain MUFAs (FA24:1, FA26:1) were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A PUFA (FA18:3) was positively associated with T2D risk.
source: For total fatty acids, three SFAs (FA12:0, FA14:0 and FA16:0) as well as a PUFA (FA18:3) were positively associated with T2D risk and two very long chain MUFAs (FA24:1, FA26:1) were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Two very long chain MUFAs (FA24:1, FA26:1) were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: For total fatty acids, three SFAs (FA12:0, FA14:0 and FA16:0) as well as a PUFA (FA18:3) were positively associated with T2D risk and two very long chain MUFAs (FA24:1, FA26:1) were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Positively associated fatty acids were mainly from DAGs and TAGs including long chain SFAs (C12-C20), MUFA (C14 and C16) and PUFA (C20 and C22).
source: Considering lipid classes, positively associated fatty acids were mainly from DAGs and TAGs including long chain SFAs (C12-C20), MUFA (C14 and C16) and PUFA (C20 and C22) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In PC and LPC classes, odd chain fatty acids (C15 and 17) were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: In contrast, in PC and LPC classes, odd chain fatty acids (C15 and 17) were negatively associated with T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the sphingolipid class, only even chain saturated and MUFAs were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: Interestingly, in the sphingolipid class, only even chain saturated and MUFAs were negatively associated with T2D risk (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Glycerolipid metabolism, which involves TAG and DAG biosynthesis, was significantly up-regulated (p=0.01).
source: Glycerolipid metabolism, which involves TAG and DAG biosynthesis, was significantly up-regulated (p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sphingolipid metabolism was found to be significantly down-regulated (p=2.11E-05).
source: In contrast, sphingolipid (p=2.11E-05), linoleic acid (p=0.016) and alpha linoleic acid (p=0.041) metabolism were found to be significantly down-regulated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Linoleic acid metabolism was found to be significantly down-regulated (p=0.016).
source: In contrast, sphingolipid (p=2.11E-05), linoleic acid (p=0.016) and alpha linoleic acid (p=0.041) metabolism were found to be significantly down-regulated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Alpha linoleic acid metabolism was found to be significantly down-regulated (p=0.041).
source: In contrast, sphingolipid (p=2.11E-05), linoleic acid (p=0.016) and alpha linoleic acid (p=0.041) metabolism were found to be significantly down-regulated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the glycerolipid biosynthesis pathway, the TAG class was increased with strong significance (p=0.003).
source: Specifically, in the glycerolipid biosynthesis pathway, the TAG class was increased with strong significance (p=0.003), suggesting an induced process of lipid storage (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The PC class of lipids was significantly reduced (p=0.015).
source: While as a whole the phospholipid metabolism pathway was not significantly altered, the PC class of lipids was significantly reduced (p=0.015) along with a modest decrease in the downstream LPC class (p<0.2), suggesting the potential inhibition of pathway from DAG to PC class.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Classes of SM (p=0.002), HCER (p=0.006) and LCER (p=0.0005) were highly reduced in sphingolipid metabolism.
source: However, classes of SM (p=0.002), HCER (p=0.006) and LCER (p=0.0005), which are downstream of sphingolipid metabolism were highly reduced, suggesting the inhibition in the process of deriving complex sphingolipids from ceramide (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A panel of 11 lipids (10 TAGs and 1 PC) was identified with excellent ability to predict future diabetes.
source: By using stepwise logistic regression modelling, we identified a panel of 11 lipids (10 TAGs and 1 PC) with excellent ability to predict future diabetes in the cohort examined (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by predictive modeling shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 11-lipid panel alone achieved a prediction ability with AUC of 0.739.
source: With these lipids alone, we achieved the prediction ability as AUC of 0.739 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: FPG showed a prediction power of AUC 0.703 which was improved to AUC 0.795 by adding lipids.
source: The classical clinic predictive parameter FPG showed the prediction power of AUC 0.703 which was improved to AUC 0.795 by adding lipids (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 2hPG showed a prediction power of AUC 0.704 which was improved to AUC 0.809 by adding lipids.
source: The clinic predictive parameter 2hPG showed the prediction power of AUC 0.704 which was improved to AUC 0.809 by adding lipids (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combination of 2hPG and FPG can achieve an AUC 0.775.
source: The combination of two clinical parameters 2hPG and FPG can achieve an AUC 0.775.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Combining the 11 lipid panel outcomes with FPG and 2hPG, the discriminative power was significantly improved to AUC 0.842.
source: Importantly, combining the 11 lipid panel outcomes with FPG and 2hPG, the discriminative power was significantly improved to AUC 0.842 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Women with recent GDM who later develop new onset T2D have clear differences in their lipidome compared to controls after delivery.
source: Importantly, our data indicate that women with recent GDM who later develop new onset T2D have clear differences in their lipidome compared to controls after delivery.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the lipidomics data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Women with recent GDM who develop T2D already exhibit lipid dysregulation in the early post-partum period.
source: This clearly shows they already exhibit lipid dysregulation in the early post-partum period.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the lipidomics data showing differences at 6-9 weeks postpartum.

claim: 91% of the lipids associated with the most significant T2D risk were TAGs (97 out of 107).
source: In addition, among the lipids associated with the most significant T2D risk, 91% of them were TAGs (97 out of 107) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the most significant lipids shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The accumulation of TAGs could be attributed to the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis.
source: Our KEGG analysis demonstrated that the glycerolipid metabolism pathway was upregulated, suggesting the accumulation of TAGs could be attributed to the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: High sugar could stimulate de novo lipogenesis in liver thereby increasing serum TAG level.
source: It was reported high sugar could stimulate de novo lipogenesis in liver thereby increasing serum TAG level (Schwarz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The elevated level of plasma hexose and insulin in incident T2D cases at baseline could be associated with enhanced endogenous lipogenesis.
source: The elevated level of plasma hexose and insulin in those incident T2D cases at baseline could be associated with the enhanced endogenous lipogenesis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting observed clinical parameters with lipid changes.

claim: The downward trend in glycerophospholipids could be linked to the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis.
source: Glycerophospholipids (through DAG) and TAGs share the same precursor glycerol-3-phosphate. Therefore, the downward trend in glycerophospholipids could be linked to the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on known metabolic pathways and observed lipid changes.

claim: Sphingolipid metabolism was the most significantly down-regulated pathway (p=2.11E-05).
source: KEGG analysis revealed that sphingolipid metabolism was the most significantly down-regulated (p=2.11E-05), further supporting the inverse association between sphingolipids and diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis.

claim: Several cross-sectional clinical studies have shown that CERs are elevated in obese subjects with T2D.
source: Several cross-sectional clinical studies have shown that CERs (upstream node of the sphingolipids pathway) are elevated in obese subjects with T2D (Meikle et al., 2013; Lemaitre et al., 2018; Lopez et al., 2013; Haus et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies have shown a negative association of SMs with diabetes risk.
source: We and others, however, have previously shown a negative association of SMs (downstream node of the whole pathway) with diabetes risk (Khan et al., 2019; Allalou et al., 2016; Razquin et al., 2018; Fall et al., 2016; Floegel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: The downward trend in glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids could be associated with the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis.
source: Therefore, in those incident T2D cases, the downward trend in glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids could be associated with the up-regulation of TAG biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on metabolic pathway relationships and observed lipid changes.

claim: Down-regulation of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids biosynthesis impairs the integrity of cell membrane structure, which might contribute to insulin resistance.
source: In addition, down-regulation of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids biosynthesis impairs the integrity of cell membrane structure, which might contribute to insulin resistance.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how lipid changes might contribute to disease.

claim: Increased TAG along with decreased phospholipids and sphingolipids could be an early sign of up-regulated endogenous de novo lipogenesis, a driving force of T2D.
source: Instead, increased TAG along with decreased phospholipids and sphingolipids could be an early sign of up-regulated endogenous de novo lipogenesis, a driving force of T2D.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the lipid profile changes observed in the study.

claim: Long chain SFA myristic acid (C14:0) and palmitic acid (C16:0) were positively associated with T2D risk.
source: Investigating the composition of the fatty acids in the lipids showed long chain SFA myristic acid (C14:0) and palmitic acid (C16:0) were positively associated with T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis.

claim: Palmitic acids were reported to cause pancreatic beta cell dysfunction and were shown to be associated with diabetes.
source: Previously, palmitic acids were reported to cause pancreatic beta cell dysfunction and were shown to be associated with diabetes (Oh et al., 2018; Nemecz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the EPIC-InterAct case, even-chain SFA in phospholipids were positively associated with diabetes risk while odd-chain SFA had a negative association.
source: A previous study on a large prospective cohort EPIC-InterAct case suggested that even-chain SFA in phospholipids were positively associated with diabetes risk while odd-chain SFA had a negative association (Forouhi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Odd-chain SFAs from phospholipids were negatively associated with T2D risk in the current study.
source: Similarly, we detected odd-chain SFA from phospholipids were negatively associated with T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis in the current study.

claim: Even-chain SFAs from glycerol lipids (TAGs and DAGs) were positively associated with T2D risk.
source: Even-chain SFAs from glycerol lipids (TAGs and DAGs) were positively associated with T2D risk while those from sphingolipids had a negative association.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis in the current study.

claim: Even-chain SFAs from sphingolipids had a negative association with T2D risk.
source: Even-chain SFAs from glycerol lipids (TAGs and DAGs) were positively associated with T2D risk while those from sphingolipids had a negative association.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis in the current study.

claim: Odd-chain SFAs (C15:0 and C17:0) are mainly exogenously derived from dairy fat intake.
source: Odd-chain SFAs (C15:0 and C17:0) are mainly exogenously derived from dairy fat intake (Smedman et al., 1999; Wolk et al., 1998; Hodson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Even-chain SFAs are from an endogenous source, such as increased lipolysis from adipose tissue or de-novo lipogenesis from excess carbohydrates.
source: In contrast, even-chain SFAs are from an endogenous source, such as increased lipolysis from adipose tissue or de-novo lipogenesis from excess carbohydrates (Hodson et al., 2008; Siler et al., 1999; Hudgins et al., 1998; King et al., 2006; Hudgins et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MUFAs, particularly those from sphingolipids, were negatively associated with T2D risk.
source: MUFAs, particularly those from sphingolipids, were negatively associated with T2D risk; however，PUFAs from TAGs were positively associated.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis in the current study.

claim: PUFAs from TAGs were positively associated with T2D risk.
source: MUFAs, particularly those from sphingolipids, were negatively associated with T2D risk; however，PUFAs from TAGs were positively associated.
evidence: This claim is supported by fatty acid composition analysis in the current study.

claim: Fatty acids from different sources and lipid classes have opposite influences on diabetes risk.
source: These findings suggest that fatty acids from different sources and lipid classes have opposite influences on diabetes risk.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the fatty acid composition analysis results.

claim: Specific metabolites of the TAG and PC classes play important roles in the early detection of women who will transition from GDM to T2D.
source: Among those 11 lipids, 10 belong to TAG and one is PC. These results suggest that specific metabolites of the TAG and PC classes play important roles in the early detection of women who will transition from GDM to T2D.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the predictive model results.

claim: Adding a specific lipidomic signature to existing clinical parameters will provide a more accurate assessment of future T2D risk.
source: Based on our data, we would envision that adding a specific lipidomic signature to existing clinical parameters for testing, perhaps including other metabolites (ie. biogenic amines and amino acids) will provide a more accurate assessment of future T2D risk.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing future applications based on the current findings.

claim: The SWIFT Study enrolled women diagnosed with GDM based on the 3 hr 100 g OGTT via Carpenter and Coustan's criteria.
source: The Study of Women, Infant Feeding, and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After GDM Pregnancy (SWIFT) is a prospective cohort that conducted in-person research exams among 1035 women with GDM diagnosed based on the 3 hr 100 g OGTT via Carpenter and Coustan's criteria, and no prior history of diabetes or other serious health conditions (age 20–45 years, diverse ethnicities) within the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Healthcare System (KPNC) (Carpenter and Coustan, 1982).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology and is supported by citation to the diagnostic criteria.

claim: Lipidomics profiling covering >1000 lipids was performed on fasting plasma samples from participants 6–9 week postpartum.
source: Lipidomics profiling covering >1000 lipids was performed on fasting plasma samples from participants 6–9 week postpartum (171 incident T2D vs. 179 controls).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study cohort, a group of triacylglycerols (low total carbon number and carbon double bonds) were found to be associated with increased risk of T2D.
source: In the Framingham Heart Study cohort, more than 100 lipid analytes were measured and a group of triacylglycerols (low total carbon number and carbon double bonds) were found to be associated with increased risk of T2D (Rhee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the PREDIMED trial, lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs), phosphatidylcholine-plasmalogens (PC-PLs), sphingomyelins (SMs), and cholesteryl esters (CEs) were found to be inversely associated with T2D risk.
source: In the PREDIMED trial, 207 plasma lipids were measured in which lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs), phosphatidylcholine-plasmalogens (PC-PLs), sphingomyelins (SMs), and cholesteryl esters (CEs) were found to be inversely associated with T2D risk while triacylglycerols (TAGs), diacylglycerol (DAGs) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PEs) were positively associated with T2D risk (Razquin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the PREDIMED trial, triacylglycerols (TAGs), diacylglycerol (DAGs) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PEs) were positively associated with T2D risk.
source: In the PREDIMED trial, 207 plasma lipids were measured in which lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs), phosphatidylcholine-plasmalogens (PC-PLs), sphingomyelins (SMs), and cholesteryl esters (CEs) were found to be inversely associated with T2D risk while triacylglycerols (TAGs), diacylglycerol (DAGs) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PEs) were positively associated with T2D risk (Razquin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In a Finnish male cohort, higher levels of specific TAGs and diacyl-phospholipids and lower levels of alkylacyl-phosphatidylcholines were observed in those who progressed to T2D.
source: In this cohort, higher levels of specific TAGs and diacyl- phospholipids and lower levels of alkylacyl-phosphatidylcholines were also observed in those who progressed to T2D (Suvitaival et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In a Chinese cohort, 38 lipids were significantly associated with T2D risk, including TAGs, LPCs, PCs, PUFA-plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamines (PUFA-PEps), and CEs.
source: In a very recent lipidomics study of a Chinese cohort, 250 lipids were tested and 38 significantly associated with T2D risk, including TAGs, LPCs, PCs, polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)–plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamines (PUFA-PEps), and CEs (Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A lipid panel including six lipids significantly improved T2D prediction compared to conventional risk factors in a Chinese cohort.
source: A lipid panel including six lipids significantly improved T2D prediction compared to that achieved by conventional risk factors (Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The positive association of TAG/DAG and T2D risk was consistently reported across multiple studies.
source: In all of these studies, the positive association of TAG/DAG and T2D risk was consistently reported.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Four lipid biomarkers (TG(51:1), TG(48:1), PC(32:1), and PCae(40:4)) were identified for GDM prediction with a moderate accuracy 71%.
source: Four lipid biomarkers (TG(51:1), TG(48:1), PC(32:1), and PCae(40:4)) were identified for GDM prediction with a moderate accuracy 71% (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A lipidomic study of women with recent GDM showed 84% accuracy in T2D prediction based on three lipids combined with six other risk factors.
source: Another lipidomic study measuring ~300 lipid species in blood samples from 104 women with recent GDM at 12 weeks post-delivery, of whom 21 cases later developed T2D, showed 84% accuracy in T2D prediction based on three lipids [i.e., PE(P-36:2), PS38:4, CE20:4] in combination with six other risk factors (i.e., age, BMI, prenatal fasting glucose, postpartum fasting glucose, total triglycerides, and total cholesterol) (Lappas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Seven lipids from early postpartum blood samples predicted later incident T2D with an AUC of 0.92 in a subset of women with recent GDM.
source: Our team identified seven lipids from early postpartum blood samples to predict later incident T2D with an AUC of 0.92 in a relatively small subset of women with recent GDM in our large prospective cohort (55 matched pairs of incident cases controls) (Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.
